models.collectorNote: NA cars with the pop-up headlights are appreciating, but a good NB is still the cheapest fun per dollar in the whole classic market. Rust behind the sills decides everything.

generations.name: First generation
generations.note: Pop-up headlights, 2,100 lb, and a brief written around one word: balance. It revived the British roadster by removing everything that made British roadsters stop working.

generations.name: Third generation
generations.note: The biggest, softest Miata — which still means small and sharp by any other standard. The power retractable hardtop made it a year-round car for northern buyers.

generations.name: Fourth generation
generations.note: Mazda cut the weight back to near-NA levels, then the 2019 update lifted the 2.0L to 181 hp and a 7,500 rpm redline. The RF hardtop targa is the looker; the soft top is the purist pick.

models.intro: The best-selling two-seat sports car in history, and the answer to almost any 'what fun car should I buy?' question. Power was never the point. Response, weight, and a roof that drops in seconds always were.
models.name: MX-5 Miata

models.collectorNote: An FD is a commitment, not a purchase. Compression numbers, cooling history, and who rebuilt the engine matter more than mileage or colour.

generations.name: First generation
generations.note: Light, simple, and rotary-powered when rotary was still a going concern. The GSL-SE's fuel-injected 13B is the one to have.

generations.name: Second generation
generations.note: The Porsche 944 of rotary cars — turbo models made up to 200 hp, and the convertible is now an underrated period piece. Handling first, straight-line speed second.

generations.name: Third generation
generations.note: Sequential twin turbos, a 2,800 lb curb weight, and styling that has not aged a day. US cars made 255 hp. Fragile if neglected, extraordinary if maintained.

models.intro: The rotary engine's masterpiece. Three generations, one idea: light weight and an engine that revs like a motorcycle. The FD is the famous one; the earlier cars are the honest bargains.
models.name: RX-7

generations.name: First generation
generations.note: The car that made Mazda matter to enthusiasts again. The Mazdaspeed3 stuffed 263 turbocharged horsepower through the front wheels and dared you to deal with the torque steer.

generations.name: Third generation
generations.note: Skyactiv efficiency, a proper interior, and handling that embarrassed German rivals. No fast version this time — the chassis always felt like it wanted one.

generations.name: Fourth generation
generations.note: Mazda chased premium: torsion-beam rear end underneath, near-luxury cabin on top. The turbo model with all-wheel drive is a grown-up hot hatch that refuses to call itself one.

models.intro: The compact for people who notice steering feel. Mazda kept giving the 3 a better interior and sharper chassis than the segment required, and the current turbo AWD car is nearly a luxury product wearing a mainstream badge.
models.name: Mazda3

generations.name: First generation
generations.note: Skyactiv's showcase: unusually good steering for a crossover, a diesel option in some markets, and styling that showed Mazda's Kodo design language could scale up.

generations.name: Second generation
generations.note: Quieter, plusher, and eventually turbocharged — the 2.5T made it a genuinely quick family car. Eight model years is a long run; it earned it.

generations.name: Third generation
generations.note: Bigger outside, more screen inside, and a hybrid version confirmed to follow the petrol launch model. Mazda is moving it slightly upmarket, as it has everything else.

models.intro: The crossover that proved family cars didn't have to steer like appliances. The CX-5 built Mazda's modern business — the profits from this car fund everything else the company makes.
models.name: CX-5
